title: Sana and the Sky-High Kite
markdown:
The Willow Creek sky blazed with colour for the annual Cloud-Kite Festival. Sana’s own rainbow kite twirled wildly, not flying straight. Nearby, Teacher Jae’s kite, painted with tiny wildflowers, caught a mischievous gust. It soared high onto the smooth steep face of Whisperwind Cliff. The cliff was a giant of rock, impossible to climb.

“Oh, my stars!” Teacher Jae sighed, shoulders slumping. The cliff seemed to dare anyone to try.

Tern, a sleek gull, landed beside them. His sharp eyes surveyed the scene. “Quite a pickle,” he squawked. “Climbing is too dangerous. And you, Sana,” he gestured to the cliff’s base, “with your feet on the ground…”

Sana chewed her lip. Her app-designer brain whirred. She’d missed the sun’s path. But as Tern spoke, she looked up. The sun cast a long shadow from the cliff’s peak, stretching all the way to them across the flat ground. Teacher Jae’s kite sat high on the face, near that peak.

A spark jumped in Sana’s eyes. She recalled a lesson about shadows. If you knew the shadow’s length and the sun’s angle, you could find an object’s height. “Tern, look at the sun hitting the cliff and that long shadow. If we measure the sun’s angle and the shadow’s length, we can find out how high the kite is.”

She grabbed her phone. “I have an app for measuring angles.”

Tern puffed out his chest. “Excellent. And I,” he tapped a strong talon, “have the best eyesight. Tell me where the shadow ends, and where the sun meets the cliff’s top.”

Sana held her phone steady. Tern’s squawks guided her, pointing out the shadow’s exact end. Sana’s app showed the sun’s altitude at a little over 40 degrees. Tern helped her measure the shadow: about 15 metres long. Height equals shadow length times the tangent of the sun’s angle. She tapped a few more things on her phone, then gasped. “It’s about 12.6 metres up. The kite is that high.”

With Sana’s precise measurement, the mountain rescue team planned their rescue from a safe distance. They used long poles from below, so no one had to climb. Soon Teacher Jae’s kite was back in her delighted hands, a bit dusty but safe.

Teacher Jae beamed. “You saved the day without climbing. You used trigonometry. It’s clever maths that helps us measure what we can’t reach, using triangles and their angles. You used the sun and shadow to find the height.”

Sana felt a thrill, not just from the rescue, but from a triangle that had been lying on the ground in plain sunlight. Tern preened his feathers. The wildflower kite, once a speck on stone, now tugged gently at Teacher Jae’s wrist. Sana’s rainbow kite still refused to fly straight. That, she decided, was a different triangle, for later.
